3131.dq: I use /…/ to enclose stem- or word-level tone melodies, e.g. /H/, /HL/, and /LH/. Such melodies can be applied to stems/words of variable syllable count. (No stress domain is defined; the tone melodies are stem/word-level, and clause-level intonation is treated separately in 3.7 Intonation contours.)

3131.prule: No word-stress rule. Word prosody is lexical tone: every noun, verb, adjective and numeral stem carries exactly one H-tone element (melodies /H/, /HL/, /LH/, /LHL/; /L/ excluded as a lexical melody), overridden by syntactically or inflectionally controlled tone overlays ({L}, {HL}, {H}). The grammar has no stress or accent section and never locates a stressed syllable.

Because there is always an H-tone, tone-dropping controlled by another word or by a suffix is always audible. The constraint does not apply to expressive adverbials, some of which have /L/ melody. [...] [3.6, p.39] I use {…} for stem- or word-level…

3131.exq_: (No stress rule. Exceptions to the one-H-per-stem tone constraint:) /HLH/ with two tonal peaks occurs in one loanword (nɔ̀y-sày) héyyɛ̀nɛ́ ‘index finger’. [...] The constraint does not apply to expressive adverbials, some of which have /L/ melody.
3131.tone: Heath 2017 describes Yorno So wholly as a tone language: stem/word-level lexical melodies /H/, /HL/, /LH/, /LHL/ with an obligatory single H-tone element per stem, plus grammatical tone overlays ({L}, {HL}, {H}) imposed by syntactic controllers and verbal inflection; a full-text search of the grammar finds 'accent' only in the p.39 remark and 'stress' only in a gloss comparison ('English unstressed now'). The only accent-related statement is the author's suspicion (p.39) that YS 'is moving in the direction of an accentual system' like Donno So and Dogul Dom, where /H/ melodies are replaced by falling /HL/; no accent placement is given. The 3.1.2 'metrical structure' remark (strong/weak positions driving Syncope/Apocope) never locates a strong syllable, and 3.4.3.1 (p.28) concludes the vowel-deletion rules track word-final position rather than 'a metrically definable position'. Hantgan 2012 (Ibi So, another Toro So variety) p.35: 'Since each verb root melody must contain at least one high tone, there is a possibility that the language could be considered pitch-accent instead of tone, with one accent per word' (speculative aside; no placement rule), and 2.3.7 (p.9-10): 'lexical tone on Noun and Verb roots is unpredictable... most verb stems have a falling tonal contour'.

3134.prule: No stress ('Ударение отсутствует'). Prosody is a four-level register tone system (extra-high a̋, high á, low à, extra-low ȁ); the tone-bearing unit is every vowel and the syllabic consonant /ŋ/; tone is both lexical and grammatical (ɗő 'go' vs ɗó 'go, habitual'). tn.translation: 2.1.2. Stress is absent. There are four level tones: extra-high (uV) a̋, high (V) á, low (N) à, extra-low (uN) ȁ. The bearer of tone is every vowel and the 'syllabic' consonant /ŋ/. Tonal distinctions are used not only for lexical but also for grammatical purposes, e.g. ɗő 'go' → ɗó 'go (habitual)' (see 2.3.5). The difference between the uV and V and between the V and N tones averages about 20 Hz, between N and uN 10 Hz. The uN tone is often accompanied by creaky-voice phonation.

3137.prule: Lexical (free, contrastive) dynamic stress: exactly one of the last three syllables of the word carries the stress, its position is not predictable by any fixed criterion, and minimal pairs are distinguished by stress position alone (káli 'wood' vs kalí 'good (pl.)', xóra 'town' vs xorá 'green'). The only constraint is the right-edge three-syllable window.
3137.srule: Only in host + enclitic groups: when a stressless enclitic is added to a word stressed on the antepenult, so that the three-syllable law would be broken, a second stress appears on the host's final syllable (o ámpele 'the vineyard' -> o ámpelé mi 'my vineyard'). Within the word itself one syllable only is stressed; no rhythmic secondary stress is described.

3138.tone: The source frames Ts'amakko prominence as TONE (H vs L), 'limited function load', placement predictable from word class / verb paradigm, default nominal melodies HL and HHL; the words 'stress' and 'pitch accent' never occur for Ts'amakko. In the same chapter the author labels Ongota's system 'accent' (§3.1.3, p. 194: penultimate in the past verb form, final in the non-past) but Ts'amakko's 'tone' (§2.1.3, p. 180), so the terminological choice is deliberate. The Köppe publisher blurb for the 2005 grammar likewise says the phonology chapter 'examines the two-tone system with its restricted functional load'. The 2005 grammar itself (§2.4.7 'Tone vs. pitch accent', published p. 34; manuscript pp. 47-48) weighs a pitch-accent analysis and rejects it: 'an analysis as pitch-accent rather than restricted tone would not simplify the analysis', concluding that the accentual features 'do not render the Ts’amakko system merely accentual'.

3139.tone: Five phonemic tones (Chao numerals 55, 33, 21, 43, 24; Table 6, sec. 5.5), with allophonic variants ([45]/[454] for 55, level~falling for 33, [11]~[21] for the low tone, [42]~[43] for 43) and falsetto phonation on 55. Limited tone sandhi (three examples from Ouyang & Zheng 1983a: 32-33, tone 24 > 33 on the first syllable of compounds), two classifiers with 55~21 variation, and 'final particles often have a neutral tone rather than their basic tone' (PT51). The only stress statements are diachronic: PC 'switch from initial to final stress in disyllabic forms' (5.1) and 'sesquisyllabic, iambically stressed, atonal... to a monosyllabic, fully tonal language' (1.2). Tsat is 'the only fully tonal Chamic language' (5.6).
3139.sec_quote: In terms of phonology, HC has restructured from a sesquisyllabic, iambically stressed, atonal (although probably marginally registral) language to a monosyllabic, fully tonal language.

The penultimate default is stated for Malagasy as a whole and applied to Tsimihety; the weak-final clause names Tsimihety explicitly.

3144.prule: No word-stress rule is stated for Tsogo in any reachable source. Tsogo is described as a tone language: two tonemes /H/ and /B/ (L) borne by every vowel; four surface realisations (high, low, falling, rising), the contours always with vowel lengthening; regular rightward tone shift ('report') of highs and lows onto the following syllable within the utterance, triggered by floating tones (a floating tone at utterance onset, two floating L before pause); vowel length is not distinctive (1991: 12). Nouns show four tone schemes /H/, /B/, /HB/, /BH/ (1991: 21 fn. 1; 2003: 380); 'In T they spread freely within a certain number of well-defined domains' (2003: 381). The only accent remark is a passing typological aside (1999: 121-122) that Getsogo and Geviya share Sesotho-like accentual characteristics (unaccented noun-class prefix immediately before a stem syllable accented by increased duration); it is not a described stress system and presents no Tsogo data.

tn.quote: MN a inventorié quatre réalisations tonales différentes: haut, bas, haut descendant et bas montant. Les deux dernières réalisations, d'après MN, s'accompagnent toujours d'un allongement de la voyelle qui les porte. Pour des raisons de simplicité, elle considère ces dernières comme des séquences de deux tons ponctuels, et ne retient ainsi que deux unités tonales minimales et distinctives: /H/ et /B/. Ces tonèmes sont associés aux phonèmes vocaliques: tout phonème vocalique est porteur d'un tonème ou d'une séquence de deux tonèmes différents.
tn.translation: MN inventoried four different tonal realisations: high, low, high-falling and low-rising. The last two, according to MN, are always accompanied by lengthening of the vowel that bears them. For simplicity she treats these as sequences of two level tones, and so retains only two minimal distinctive tonal units: /H/ and /B/ [L]. These tonemes are associated with the vowel phonemes: every vowel phoneme bears one toneme or a sequence of two different tonemes.

3149.dq: Stress falls on the first syllable of the root of a word.
3149.dloc: Sec. 1 'Phonology', p. 8 (page per the work's own table of contents, '1 Phonology 8'; read on p. 1 of the Rosetta Project excerpt, archive.org, which carries no page number)
3149.prule: Stress falls on the first syllable of the root of the word; prefixes (reciprocal ang-, reduplicant me-) are unstressed, so the stressed syllable is located by morphological structure, not by counting from a word edge (ang-me-'mengen-ai 'discuss' has stress on the third syllable of the word). Stated exception: derived adverbs, formed with the causative prefix a- on an adjective or a verb, are stressed on the prefix ('a-ro 'well', p. 8); this stress distinguishes the adverb from the causative transitive verb, which keeps root stress (adverb 'a-tung vs. verb a-'tung 'stand it up', p. 31).
3149.srule: Not mentioned in Fast 1990, sec. 1 'Phonology' (p. 8), nor in Fast 1992 Tungag OPD, 'Suprasegmentals' (p. 3).
3149.quote: Each of the consonants has a phonemically contrastive lengthened counterpart. These will be written as double consonants (e.g. kk, ll, etc.) except for v and r, whose lengthened forms will be written b and d respectively. Stress falls on the first syllable of the root of a word. 1) ang-me-'mengen-ai Recip-Redup-talk-? 3151.prule: Word stress falls as the norm on the last syllable of the word ('Der Akzent ruht als Norm auf der letzten Silbe des Wortes'), stated without any weight condition; a closed list of unstressable elements leaves the accent on the syllable before them (Persian izafat -i and indefinite/relative -ī, the imperative person suffixes other than 2sg, the 1pl aorist person marker, negative -mA, the copular 'esse' suffixes also in certain tenses, the present-tense predicate suffixes, the verbal suffix -in; also the copula particles u 'und' and ta), some Persian loans (bä'lī 'ja') and some Turkic adverbs and imperatives (bō'ra 'hier', ye'pi 'iß') keep non-final accent, the vocative shifts the accent to the first syllable (bū'zäk 'Eis!'), and strong emphasis shifts or levels the accent (qā'ni). Rules established on the Xarrab dialect and said to hold for the other Khalaj dialects.
3151.srule: No secondary stress within the word is described. Main vs secondary accent (Haupt-/Nebenakzent) is treated only at word-group level: the grammatical role of the words decides which word carries the main and which the secondary accent (päsänd yetmä'k 'mögen' vs päsä'nd yeti` 'möge!').
